params.question: A 50-year-old diabetic presents with a generalised tonic-clonic seizure during an episode of severe hypoglycaemia (blood glucose 35 mg/dL). Which of the following correctly explains why this event alone does not qualify as epilepsy?

answers.text: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures are convulsions, not true seizures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A convulsion is a motor subtype of seizure. A generalised tonic-clonic event is both a seizure and a convulsion — the terms are not mutually exclusive.

answers.text: This is a provoked seizure; the ILAE criteria require unprovoked seizures for an epilepsy diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This seizure was triggered by acute hypoglycaemia — a reversible metabolic cause. The ILAE 2014 definition requires unprovoked seizures. The right approach is to treat the hypoglycaemia, not start antiepileptic drugs.

answers.text: A single seizure always requires a second episode before epilepsy can be diagnosed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not always. Even a single unprovoked seizure with a ≥60% recurrence risk over ten years can satisfy the ILAE criteria. The key issue here is that this seizure is provoked, not that it is a single episode.
Severe hypoglycaemia can cause genuine seizures through neuronal energy failure. The generalised tonic-clonic movements described here are a seizure, not syncope.

overallFeedback.feedback: This seizure was provoked by acute hypoglycaemia. The ILAE 2014 criteria require unprovoked seizures for epilepsy. A provoked seizure needs treatment of the underlying cause, not antiepileptic drugs.

Correct! Provoked seizures due to reversible causes such as hypoglycaemia do not meet the ILAE 2014 criteria for epilepsy. Treat the cause first — antiepileptic drugs are reserved for unprovoked recurrence.

params.question: A normal electroencephalogram (EEG) result rules out the diagnosis of epilepsy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: A normal EEG does not rule out epilepsy. The EEG captures electrical activity only during the recording period, and many patients with epilepsy have normal interictal recordings. Sleep deprivation and photic stimulation can improve the yield.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct! A normal interictal EEG does not exclude epilepsy. Many patients have entirely normal recordings between seizures. Sleep deprivation and photic stimulation improve the diagnostic yield of the EEG.

params.question: Which of the following best explains why benzodiazepines become progressively less effective during prolonged status epilepticus?

answers.text: Hepatic metabolism of benzodiazepines accelerates during prolonged seizures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hepatic metabolism is not the primary reason for benzodiazepine failure in status epilepticus. The mechanism is at the receptor level in the brain, not at the metabolic level in the liver.

answers.text: GABA-A receptors are progressively internalised from the synaptic membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. During prolonged seizures, inhibitory GABA-A receptors are removed from the synapse through receptor internalisation. This reduces the target available for benzodiazepines, explaining why the status epilepticus protocol mandates timely escalation to second-line agents.

answers.text: Benzodiazepines are redistributed to adipose tissue during prolonged infusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Drug redistribution is a general pharmacokinetic phenomenon but is not the primary mechanism for benzodiazepine failure in status epilepticus. The key change is progressive loss of GABA-A receptors from the neuronal membrane.

answers.text: Voltage-gated sodium channels become permanently inactivated, blocking drug access

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sodium channels are involved in focal seizure propagation, but their inactivation is not the mechanism behind benzodiazepine failure. The issue is progressive removal of GABA-A receptors from the synaptic surface.

overallFeedback.feedback: During prolonged status epilepticus, GABA-A receptors are progressively removed from the synaptic membrane. This receptor internalisation makes benzodiazepines less effective the longer a seizure continues — and is the reason the protocol must escalate on time, not on hope.

Correct! GABA-A receptor internalisation during prolonged seizures is why benzodiazepines lose effectiveness — and why the status epilepticus protocol mandates timely escalation to second-line agents rather than repeated benzodiazepine doses.

params.question: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy well-controlled on sodium valproate is planning pregnancy. What is the most appropriate counselling regarding her medication?

answers.text: Continue valproate throughout pregnancy as seizure control is the top priority

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Seizure control matters, but sodium valproate is the most teratogenic commonly used AED. It causes neural tube defects and must be switched to a safer alternative before conception.

answers.text: Switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam and start high-dose folic acid before conception

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Sodium valproate causes neural tube defects — the most important AED safety issue in women of childbearing age. Before planned pregnancy, switch to a safer agent and begin high-dose folic acid supplementation.

answers.text: Stop all antiepileptic drugs immediately to protect the foetus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Abruptly stopping AEDs risks breakthrough seizures and potentially status epilepticus, which is dangerous for both mother and foetus. The correct approach is a supervised switch to a safer drug, not abrupt withdrawal.

answers.text: Switch to carbamazepine as it has the best safety profile in pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that reduces the efficacy of hormonal contraception and carries its own teratogenic risk. Lamotrigine or levetiracetam are the preferred alternatives when planning pregnancy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Sodium valproate causes neural tube defects and is the most critical AED safety issue for women of childbearing age. Before planned pregnancy, switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam and start high-dose folic acid — never stop all AEDs abruptly.

Correct! Valproate teratogenicity is the most important AED safety concern in clinical practice. The standard approach is to switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam and start high-dose folic acid before conception.
